topic: How AI agent swarms actually work when the models run locally on Ollama
title: An Agent Swarm Runs on One Local Model
description: Working description: how an AI agent swarm coordinates, and how to point it at your own Ollama server so tokens cost electricity instead of dollars.
hook_candidates: You've got Ollama running. A swarm is one line away.
Three agents. One model. No per-token bill.
Thousands of agents, says Karpathy. You can't wire three.
A swarm isn't many models. It's turns.
One model, many roles, zero token bills.
Your Ollama box could run a swarm tonight.
Two dollars per million tokens, or your wall socket.
Every agent in the swarm is the same model.
Swarms aren't magic. They're group chat.
Stop renting agents. Your GPU already is one.
narration_full: A swarm isn't many models. It's a single model taking turns. You already run that model in Ollama, and a swarm sounds like a pile of extra machines. An agent is your Ollama chat with a name, a role, and tools. The same model answers as each agent. Every agent is that same model taking turns. So who speaks next? AutoGen's SelectorGroupChat hands that choice to a model. It reads the shared conversation and picks the next speaker. Each reply is broadcast to the whole team. A stop word or message cap, the termination condition, ends the run. OpenAI's Agents SDK does it with a tool call. A handoff, one agent passing the task, is a tool called transfer to refund agent. LangGraph instead shares one state, a common board every agent reads and writes. Every framework points at a base U R L, the address for model requests. Set it to localhost, port eleven thousand four hundred thirty-four. One line re-points the swarm to your Ollama server. The client demands an A P I key; Ollama ignores it. The deeper change is the bill. G P T six point one Sol charges two dollars per million input tokens, chunks of text. A swarm re-sends its conversation with every turn. Every message between agents pays that meter. Your box never meters a token. NVIDIA's D G X Spark, built for this workload, ships with a two hundred forty watt power supply. Cloud charges per plate. Your box is a buffet, stove already on. The buffet has a single stove, though. Ollama serves a single request at a time by default, and extra parallel slots cost memory. Your agents take turns. Want them at once? Then the myth has a point: parallelism costs memory. The honest catch: MAST, the largest published audit of multi-agent failures. It annotated traces of real swarm runs across the popular frameworks. It sorted them into fourteen failure modes, mostly coordination, not weak models. So a local swarm buys you unlimited cheap tokens, not unlimited good ones.

analogy.vehicle: cloud per-plate billing versus a buffet with the stove already on
analogy.mapping: cloud APIs charge per token like a la carte; the local box is flat-rate because the model is already loaded
analogy.limit: the buffet has one stove: requests queue by default and parallelism is paid in RAM

notes_for_review: One analogy: cloud per-plate billing versus a buffet with the stove already on (s07), with its limit stated at the top of s08, one stove so requests queue and memory is the real cap. Key numbers spent on screen: $2.00 / 1M input tokens (s06), 240 W (s07), 14 failure modes (s10); the sixteen hundred traces are spoken only, and port 11434 is shown so it is spoken. Hedged by omission: no local cents-per-token figure and no Karpathy line, both Unverified in the brief; used the bare localhost:11434 form per the brief's endpoint note, and dropped the termination-condition step for time.
